newsitem.title: ITALY: English gentleman is Milan vogue with a difference.
newsitem.headline: English gentleman is Milan vogue with a difference.

text.p: Casual and sporty, the English country gentleman is back in vogue but forget stiff tweeds and scratchy Shetland wools -- autumn designs have a much more luxurious dimension.

Tweeds, flannels and velvets were the look at this week's Milan ready-to-wear shows, with slimfit tailoring coming even from top Italian designer Giorgio Armani, so long famed for broad shouldered suits which accentuated male dimensions.
But designers have worked soft mohair and alpaca wool into British fabrics to give autumn/winter 1997/98 a finer feel.

"There is the return to the English country gentleman but in a very updated way because the colours are very rich and the fabrics they're using are rich," said Fiona Firth, menswear fashion buyer for exclusive London store Harvey Nichols.

"People are using tweed effects, Shetland wools, corduroy and velvet. But it's not like traditional English fabrics that are really stiff because a lot of them are very soft, they've got mohair in them and alpaca so the drape is there," she said.
Jonathan Akeroyd, men's designer collection buyer at another exclusive London store Harrods, said many designers were stressing quality, with existing shapes little changed.
"There's been emphasis on styling and detail from people like (U.S. designer) Donna Karan. There's not so much radical change but emphasis on cashmere and leather," he said.
Casual attire is growing and comfort a key factor, with jackets like cardigans and the return of the sports jacket.

"People won't be buying suits as such, they'll be putting mixes together like a corduroy jacket with a velvet check jean or a flat-front trouser. Shirts aren't really important. Fine gauge and chunky knitwear is coming back," Firth said.

Karan said after her show this week that menswear had so far lacked choice in sporty outfits. "Every principle that I have ever felt about menswear is what this collection is all about -- soft, stretch, comfort, tailoring, the body," she said.
Akeroyd noted stretch fabric played a major role although customers were still unused to, it especially in suits.
"The customer hasn't really experienced it - it's still very new. It only hit the big time in the last two or three seasons and most people haven't actually got it on their backs yet."
Designers had tweaked styles after recent collections of narrow shoulders and waists but buyers said they had seen little that was startlingly new.
Firth said instead collections like that of Italian design duo Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana had a coherency which made them simple to present to the customer in the store.

"Dolce & Gabbana is easy to put together, the shapes are good -- it's nothing new but Dolce & Gabbana have become a bit of a classic now, people know their shape. If it's easy for us to put together the customer will understand it straightaway."

In a week which saw theatrical 16th century doublets and hose from Briton Vivienne Westwood and autumnal hues like rust, chocolate and bottle green dominating colours, U.S. stylist Tom Ford at fashion house Gucci was one big name to make style innovations, dropping a previous narrow shouldered look.
"The jacket was a lot wider and the trouser was like an Oxford bag. Shoulder blades were a lot longer and bigger - so a big change from Gucci," Akeroyd said.
